title: Uniform, Exponential, Gamma, Beta and Log-Normal
objectives: Compute probabilities under a uniform distribution and recognise when it models 'no information'
Use the exponential distribution for waiting times, including its survival function and memorylessness
Describe gamma as a sum of exponentials and beta as a distribution on probabilities with updating
Explain why prices are log-normal when log-returns are normal, and compute median and mean price factors
motivation: Not everything in finance is normal. Waiting times to the next default follow an exponential; the time until the third jump is gamma; an estimated default probability is beta-distributed; and prices themselves are log-normal - which is exactly why \$100 can fall to \$50 but never to -\$50. This lesson is the toolkit for the shapes that are not bell curves.

blocks.text: Uniform: honest ignorance on an interval

blocks.md: The **uniform** on $[a, b]$ spreads probability evenly: constant density $1/(b-a)$, so the probability of a sub-interval is just its length over $(b - a)$. Use it when you genuinely know only a range: the moment within the next minute that a quote refresh will land, or a fill price constrained to a known spread band. Its mean sits at the midpoint $(a+b)/2$ and its variance is $(b-a)^2/12$.

blocks.title: Worked example: uniform on [0, 10]
items: $P(X > 7 \mid X > 5) = 3/5 = 0.6$ - conditioning on $X > 5$ shrinks the effective interval to $[5, 10]$ (compare with the exponential below: uniform is **not** memoryless).

blocks.text: Exponential: waiting for the first jump

blocks.md: The **exponential($\lambda$)** models the waiting time $T$ until the first event of a Poisson process - the first default, the next jump, the next order arrival - when events arrive at constant rate $\lambda$ per unit time. Its key formulas are worth memorising in survival form:

blocks.caption: Exponential survival function, mean and median

blocks.title: Worked example: time to default at hazard 0.5/year
items: Hazard $\lambda = 0.5$ defaults per year; expected time to default $= 1/0.5 = 2$ years.
Survival past 2 years: $P(T > 2) = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$ - about a 37% chance of no default within two years.
Median: $\ln 2 / 0.5 \approx 1.3863$ years - half of such assets default sooner than this.
Memoryless: $P(T > 3 \mid T > 1) = P(T > 2) = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$ - surviving one year does not age the asset; the hazard stays $\lambda$.

blocks.title: Memorylessness is a modelling choice, not a law
blocks.md: The exponential's constant hazard fits newly issued instruments with stable credit quality, but real default risk often rises with leverage build-up and macro deterioration - a rising hazard needs models from the stochastic-processes module. The exponential is the cleanest baseline because 'no memory' makes every future interval identical, which is why it pairs with the Poisson count model of the distributions lesson: exponential gaps between Poisson events.

blocks.text: Gamma and Beta: the builders' distributions

blocks.md: The **gamma($k, \lambda$)** distribution is the waiting time until the $k$-th event of the same Poisson process - a sum of $k$ independent exponentials. With shape $k$ and rate $\lambda$ its mean is $k/\lambda$. The **beta($\alpha, \beta$)** distribution lives on $[0, 1]$ and is the natural model for a probability or fraction: it is flexible from uniform ($\alpha = \beta = 1$) to heavily skewed, and it updates from data by simple arithmetic - observe successes and failures, add them to the parameters. This makes it the standard prior in Bayesian estimation of a default rate.

blocks.title: Worked example: third default and beta updating
items: Gamma: time $T_3$ until the 3rd default, $\lambda = 0.5$/year. Mean $= 3/0.5 = 6$ years.
Probability the 3rd default takes longer than 4 years = probability of fewer than 3 events in 4 years, where the event count is Poisson with $\lambda t = 2$: $P = e^{-2}(1 + 2 + 2) \approx 0.6767$.
Beta: prior belief on a default rate $\text{Beta}(2, 8)$ has mean $2/10 = 0.20$.
Observe 3 defaults in 10 loans: posterior $\text{Beta}(2 + 3, 8 + 7) = \text{Beta}(5, 15)$, mean $5/20 = 0.25$ - the data nudged the estimate up from 20% to 25%.

blocks.md: If the **log-return** of an asset over a period is normal, $\ln(S_T/S_0) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, then the price ratio $S_T/S_0$ is **log-normal**: always positive and right-skewed. This is the right model for prices because it respects the one hard constraint markets have - prices cannot go negative - and it matches compounding: multiplying many independent period returns sums their logs, and the CLT then makes the log normal. Two facts to keep straight:

blocks.caption: Log-normal median and mean price factors

blocks.title: Worked example: one-year price factors
items: Model: annual log-return $\sim N(0.05, 0.2^2)$ - 5% log-drift, 20% log-volatility.
Median outcome: $e^{0.05} \approx 1.0513$ - half of years end above a 5.1% price gain, half below.
Mean outcome: $e^{0.05 + 0.02} = e^{0.07} \approx 1.0725$ - the extra $\sigma^2/2 = 0.02$ is volatility's contribution to the average, driven by the right tail's big up-years.
Chance of a down year: $P(S_T < S_0) = P(\ln(S_T/S_0) < 0) = \Phi((0 - 0.05)/0.2) = \Phi(-0.25) \approx 0.4013$.
Read that carefully: positive drift, yet the price falls in about 40% of years - because half the distribution sits below the median, which is above 1 only by the drift.

blocks.caption: The exponential at hazard 0.5: the survival curve decays like e^{-0.5t}, mean 2 and median about 1.39 - the median sits left of the mean because of the long right tail.

blocks.code:
from math import exp, erf, sqrt

phi = lambda z: 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2)))
print(round(exp(0.05), 4), round(exp(0.07), 4))   # median and mean price factors
print(round(phi(-0.25), 4))                        # P(S_T < S_0)
blocks.caption: The log-normal computations from the worked example.

guidedExercise.prompt: A machine's time to failure is exponential with rate $\lambda = 0.25$ failures per year. Compute (a) $P(\text{survives past 4 years})$, (b) the expected lifetime, (c) the median lifetime, and (d) $P(\text{survives past 5 years} \mid \text{has survived 1 year})$.
hints: Memorylessness: given survival to time 1, the remaining wait restarts the same exponential.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$. (b) $1/0.25 = 4$ years. (c) $\ln 2/0.25 \approx 2.7726$ years. (d) By memorylessness, $P(T > 5 \mid T > 1) = P(T > 4) = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$ - the extra year of survival does not age the machine.

independentExercise.prompt: A stock trades in a band modelled as uniform on [90, 110] for the next tick. (a) Compute $P(\text{price} > 105)$ and the mean price. (b) Jumps arrive at Poisson rate $\lambda = 0.5$ per hour - what is the probability of no jump in the next hour, and how does it connect to the exponential waiting time?
hints: (a) Probability is length of the favourable interval over 20.
(b) 'No jump in an hour' equals 'waiting time exceeds 1 hour'.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $P = (110 - 105)/20 = 0.25$; mean $= 100$. (b) $P(N(1) = 0) = e^{-0.5} \approx 0.6065$, which is exactly the exponential survival probability $P(T > 1)$ with rate 0.5 - the count and waiting-time views are two sides of the same process.

commonMistakes: Treating a uniform variable as memoryless - uniform on [0,10] forgets nothing: conditioning on X > 5 shifts the remaining distribution.
Confusing the exponential's rate $\lambda$ with its mean: the mean is $1/\lambda$, so a rate of 0.5 per year means a 2-year average wait.
Adding the sigma^2/2 term to the median instead of the mean of a log-normal - the median factor is e^mu exactly.
Modelling prices directly as normal: it admits negative prices; model log-returns as normal and prices become log-normal.
realWorldApplication: Customer service wait times, equipment failure times and radioactive decay all follow exponential-type survival curves; Bayesian A/B testing and quality estimation use beta updating for proportions and rates.
quantFinanceApplication: Credit models use exponential hazards for time-to-default, gamma/Erlang for timing of the k-th default in first-to-default baskets, beta priors for estimated default rates, and the log-normal price model underlies the Black-Scholes assumption $\ln(S_T/S_0) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with the mean factor $e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$.
summary: Uniform on $[a,b]$: probability = length ratio; mean at the midpoint; no memorylessness.
Exponential($\lambda$): $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$, mean $1/\lambda$, median $\ln 2/\lambda$, memoryless - the time to the first Poisson event.
Gamma($k, \lambda$): waiting time to the $k$-th event, mean $k/\lambda$; beta($\alpha, \beta$): distribution on $[0,1]$ updated by adding observed successes and failures.
Log-normal prices: $\ln(S_T/S_0) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ gives median factor $e^{\mu}$, mean factor $e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$, and positivity by construction.
Count and waiting-time views are linked: exponential gaps generate Poisson counts.

quiz.prompt: A waiting time $T$ is exponential with rate $\lambda = 0.5$ per year. What is $P(T > 2)$? (4 decimal places.)
An exponential variable has already survived past time 3. What is the distribution of its **remaining** wait?
options: A different exponential with a smaller rate - it has aged
The same exponential - memorylessness restarts the clock
It depends on how close to the mean the survival time was
quiz.explanation: Memorylessness: $P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = P(T > t)$. Survival does not change the hazard, so the remaining wait is a fresh exponential with the same rate.

quiz.prompt: For an exponential with rate $\lambda = 0.5$ per year, what is the median waiting time in years? (4 decimal places.)
quiz.explanation: Median $= \ln 2 / \lambda = 0.6931/0.5 \approx 1.3863$ - well below the mean of 2 because of the right skew.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
from math import exp, erf, sqrt
phi = lambda z: 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2)))
print(round(exp(0.05), 4), round(exp(0.07), 4))
print(round(phi(-0.25), 4))
quiz.explanation: Median factor $e^{0.05}$, mean factor $e^{0.05 + 0.2^2/2} = e^{0.07}$, and the probability of a down year $\Phi(-0.25)$ - the log-normal worked example.

quiz.prompt: Why are prices modelled as log-normal rather than normal?
options: Log-normal prices have a lower mean
Log-normal variables are always positive and right-skewed, matching compounding and the no-negative-prices constraint
Log-normal distributions have thinner tails than normal ones
quiz.explanation: Prices cannot go below zero, and multiplicative compounding of returns corresponds to adding log-returns - which the CLT makes normal, forcing the price ratio to be log-normal. Its tail is fatter (right-skewed), not thinner.

quiz.prompt: With annual log-return $\sim N(0.05, 0.2^2)$, what is $P(S_T < S_0)$, using $\Phi(-0.25) = 0.4013$? (4 decimal places.)
quiz.explanation: $P(S_T < S_0) = P(\ln(S_T/S_0) < 0) = \Phi((0 - 0.05)/0.2) = \Phi(-0.25) \approx 0.4013$ - about 40% of years are down despite positive drift.

flashcards.back: $P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = P(T > t)$ - the exponential (continuous) and geometric (discrete) are the only memoryless distributions.
Gamma($k$, $\lambda$) is the time to the k-th event of a rate-$\lambda$ Poisson process - a sum of k iid exponentials; mean $k/\lambda$.
Prior Beta(alpha, beta) on a probability + observe s successes and f failures = posterior Beta(alpha + s, beta + f). Beta(2,8) + 3 defaults in 10 loans = Beta(5,15).
If $\ln(S_T/S_0) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$: median factor $e^{\mu}$; mean factor $e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$.
